newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Tung seeks to mend rift with Democrats.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung seeks to mend rift with Democrats.

text.p: Hong Kong's chief executive-designate Tung Chee-hwa extended an olive branch to the popular Democratic Party on Thursday with offers of regular dialogue and an open line to emergency meetings.

But the gulf between both sides remained wide with the party's refusal to support an interim lawmaking chamber handpicked by Beijing that China plans to put in place of Hong Kong's elected legislature upon the handover on July 1.

"We hope to have such a meeting with Mr Tung (once) every two months. And if emergencies arise, we would like to ask for emergency meetings," incumbent legislator and head of Democratic Party, Martin Lee, told reporters after his meeting with Tung.
"Mr Tung accepted the suggestion. The next meeting will be taking place in the early part of March," he said.
Tung, who was meeting the democrats for the first time since his selection as the British territory's first post-colonial leader, said he recognised the importance of constant dialogue.
"I am afraid we have rather different views. I think it is necessary to continue the dialogue," he told reporters.
The one-and-a-half hour meeting, described as frank and cordial by both sides, also focussed on problems of new Chinese immigrants to Hong Kong, the elderly and housing.

But differences became evident when the party stood firm in opposing the provisional legislature and threatened to sue the body should it try to pass laws before Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule this year, Lee said.
"We told Mr Tung that if the provisional legislature attempts to legislate or to pass laws before July 1 then we will have no option but to take it to court," he said.

Formed in December under the careful supervision of China, the provisional legislature is made up of staunchly pro-Beijing figures including several who were defeated in Hong Kong's last legislative election.
A pro-Beijing panel of 400, which put together the chamber, also selected Tung as Hong Kong's future chief executive.

Thursday's meeting came after Tung hit out at critics of the provisional chamber, saying those who tried to lobby for Western support in condemning the body were doing a disservice to fellow residents of the territory.

In the past year, Lee and other prominent pro-democracy figures have made several trips abroad to lobby Western leaders to condemn the China-backed chamber as a contravention of Sino-British handover treaties.

"I hope they will not make further negative comment, especially to foreigners because they don't understand the complexities of the provisional legislature," Tung said after meeting Lee and his party colleagues.

"They did say they would challenge the legality of the provisional legislature in court. I told them it is not in the interest of Hong Kong and the interest of the 6.3 million Hong Kong people," he said.
Lee said the party had assured Tung it would participate in the next election, expected to be held in 1998.
